body.p: Claims 1-15 are pending in this application upon entry of this Amendment. In this Amendment, the Applicant has rewritten claim 8 as an independent claim. No claims have been cancelled or added in this Amendment. Claims 1 and 8-9 are independent claims.

The Examiner rejected claims 1 and 8-10 under 35 U.S.C. § 102 as being anticipated by U.S. Publication No. 2015/0375857 ("Swanson"). The Applicant respectfully traverses these rejections for at least the following reasons.
Independent claim 1 is reproduced below (Applicant emphasis added):
1. A flight control system that is adapted
for controlling movements of a rotary wing aircraft,
comprising:
sensors that are configured to generate sensor
data based on captured motions of the rotary wing
aircraft;

p.u: motion actuators that are adapted for inducing

body.p: a translational and/or a rotational movement of the rotary wing aircraft about at least one of a yaw axis,
a roll axis, or a pitch axis; and
a passenger discomfort-aware control unit that

is configured to receive the sensor data from the sensors and to generate, based on the sensor data, passenger discomfort-aware actuator control signals for controlling the motion actuators of the rotary wing aircraft, wherein the passenger discomfort-aware actuator control signals are at least suitable for kinetosis reduction or for whole-body vibration reduction in passengers of the rotary-wing aircraft when

p.u: being applied to the motion actuators.

body.p: As set forth, in independent claim 1, a passenger discomfort-aware control unit generates, based on sensed motion of a rotary wing aircraft, passenger discomfort-aware actuator

control signals for controlling motion actuators that are adapted for inducing translational and/or rotational movements of the aircraft, the passenger discomfort-aware actuator control signals being suitable for kinetosis or whole-body vibration reduction in passengers of the aircraft when applied to the motion actuators.
At the outset, the Applicant notes that references cited in the Office Action either

(i) relate to onboard vibration limiters as Swanson, and as U.S. Publication No. 2005/0240326 ("Lauwerys") discussed below, without aiming at overcoming passenger discomfort based upon simulation results or (ii) relate to simulators, as Korean Publication No. 20210019661 ("Seo") and U.S. Publication No. 2017/0243505 ("Dimock") both discussed below, not intended to address such passenger discomfort. Therefore, motivation for a person skilled of the art to combine teachings from Swanson/Lauwerys with the teachings of Seo/Dimock would be lacking.

Turning now to a comparison of independent claim 1 and Swanson, Swanson describes actively controlling vibration in a rotary winged aircraft (paragraph [0003] of Swanson). Swanson's purpose is to control vibrations that can damage the aircraft, to limit costs associated with inspecting and replacing aircraft parts becoming damaged during vibration, as opposed to controlling translational and/or rotational movements of the aircraft to reduce passenger discomfort pursuant to independent claim 1.

As per Swanson, an aircraft system 10 uses information obtained from an aircraft avionics system, links, and/or a data bus to control vibration imposed by a rotor system 30. Aircraft system 10 includes an active vibration control (AVC) 20 adapted to control vibration imposed by rotor system 30. AVC 20 uses information from an aircraft avionics system 40, configured to sense, measure, and detect vibrations and receives real-time aircraft information from a data bus/link. AVC 20 has an adjust algorithm to control parameters as a function of real-time aircraft information, and to calculate a force command. Then, AVC 20 generates a force that reduces vibrations imposed by rotor system 30 thereby actively counteracting aircraft vibration (paragraph [0028] of Swanson).

AVCS 20 includes sensors 22, a controller 24, and actuators 26. Actuators 26 are located on the rotor blades and at the bottom floor of the cabin of the aircraft, as illustrated in FIG. 1 of Swanson, reproduced as follows:

Swanson fails to teach or suggest any "passenger" or "person" being the object for the vibration cancelling. Swanson simply aims avoiding fatigue and wear on equipment, materials, and occupants (one occurrence in paragraph [0003] of Swanson) within the aircraft. Thus, Swanson fails to teach or suggest a passenger discomfort-aware control unit pursuant to independent claim 1.

Furthermore, Swanson does not mention motion actuators adapted for inducing translational and/or rotational movements of the aircraft, pursuant to independent claim 1, as its actuators generate local vibrations counteracting other deleterious ones.

Moreover, Swanson fails to teach or suggest generating, based on sensor data, passenger discomfort-aware actuator control signals pursuant to independent claim 1. Thus, Swanson fails to teach or suggest such discomfort-aware signals for controlling motion actuators in a rotary wing aircraft that would be suitable for kinetosis reduction or for whole-body vibration reduction in passengers when being applied, pursuant to independent claim 1.

Consequently, for at least the above reasons, Swanson does not teach or suggest all features of independent claim 1. Accordingly, independent claim 1 is patentable over Swanson. For similar reasoning, rewritten independent claim 8 and independent claim 9 are also patentable over Swanson. Claims 2-7 depend from independent claim 1 and claims 10-15 depend from independent claim 9. Claims 2-7 and 10-15 are therefore also patentable over Swanson.

The Examiner rejected claims 2-3 and 6-7 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being obvious over Swanson in view of U.S. Publication No. 2005/0240326 ("Lauwerys"). Claims 2-3 and 6-7 depend from independent claim 1 and are therefore patentable over Swanson in view of Lauwerys.

Furthermore, Lauwerys relates to vehicle suspension systems. Lauwerys describes controlling a shock absorber system of a road vehicle, i.e., a "passenger car" (paragraph [0003] of Lauwerys). A semi-active shock absorber 20 having a rod 24, a cylinder 22, and an accumulator 31 is provided. In shock absorber 20, the classical piston and base valves are each replaced by a check valve, i.e., by a piston check valve 28 and a base check valve 30. A current controlled continually variable semi-active ("CVSA") valve 32 is also provided. A controller 33 generates an input current for CVSA valve 32, with values which corresponds to open and closed positions of valve 32, respectively (paragraph [0023] of Lauwerys).

In operation of the passenger car, when rod 24 moves up piston check valve 28 closes and oil flows through valve 32. Because the volume of rod 24 inside cylinder 22 reduces, oil is forced from accumulator 31 into cylinder 22 through base check valve 30. The rattle displacement/velocity is the relative displacement/velocity of rod 24 with respect to cylinder 22 (paragraph [0024] of Lauwerys). When rod 24 moves down, piston check valve 28 opens. Because the volume of rod 24 inside cylinder 22 increases, base check-valve 30 closes and oil flows from cylinder 22 into accumulator 31 through CVSA valve 32.

A linear controller consisting of several feedback and feedforward modules, each tackling a specific comfort or handling issue, is provided. The output of the modules is summed to a desired modal virtual damper force. The goal is to suppress the modal motions of the passenger car to increase the comfort of the passengers (paragraph [0051] of Lauwerys). An integral feedback controller determines the average amount of damping in the system (paragraph [0059] of Lauwerys).

In Lauwerys, a bilinear model implements a bilinear approximation which turns out to be more linearizing for broadband excitation signals, such as stochastic road excitations. The bilinear damper model includes only one parameter, "i0", while the lookup table damper model consists of a large amount of data points to describe the nonlinear characteristics of the damper. (paragraph [0044] of Lauwerys).
As set forth, Lauwerys fails to teach or suggest a rotary wing aircraft pursuant to independent claim 1 as Lauwerys relates to damping characteristic of the shock absorbers in road vehicles.

Besides, Lauwerys does not mention actuators adapted for inducing translational and/or rotational movements of the vehicle pursuant to independent claim 1 as the dampers simply act as shock absorbers.

Moreover, Lauwerys is silent about controlling motion actuators in a rotary wing aircraft that would be suitable for kinetosis reduction in passengers when being applied, pursuant to independent claim 1.

The Examiner rejected claim 4 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being obvious over Swanson in view of Lauwerys and Korean Publication No. 20210019661 ("Seo"). Claim 4 depends from independent claim 1 and is therefore patentable over Swanson in view of Lauwerys and Seo.

Furthermore, Seo describes a structural interlocking test for improving stability and piloting performance of an aircraft. Seo provides designing a digital flight control rule, receiving an FEM model of an aircraft airframe, receiving a reaction model by an actuator from the FEM model of the aircraft airframe, and generating a structural interlocking plant model including the FEM model of the aircraft airframe and the reaction model by the driving unit. Seo provides analyzing the structural interlocking test model using a frequency input according to a flight condition as a reference input and creates a structural interlocking filter. Seo uses a variable gain regulator to design and verify a filter which can check a structural interlocking phenomenon and improve stability.

Seo fails to teach or suggest any "passenger" or "person." Seo simply aims improving in-flight stability and piloting performance. Thus, Seo fails to teach or suggest a passenger discomfort-aware control unit pursuant to independent claim 1.

Besides, Seo does not mention actuators adapted for inducing translational and/or rotational movements of the vehicle, pursuant to independent claim 1, as the actuator motions are only adapted based upon the model.

Moreover, Seo fails to teach or suggest generating, based on sensor data, passenger discomfort-aware actuator control signals pursuant to independent claim 1. Thus, Seo fails to teach or suggest such discomfort-aware signals for controlling motion actuators in a rotary wing aircraft
that would be suitable for kinetosis reduction or for whole-body vibration reduction in passengers when being applied, pursuant to independent claim 1.

The Examiner rejected claim 5 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being obvious over Swanson in view of Lauwerys, Seo, and U.S. Publication No. 2017/0243505 ("Dimock"). Claim 5 depends from independent claim 1 and is therefore patentable over Swanson in view of Lauwerys, Seo, and Dimock.

Furthermore, Dimock describes adaptive control for flight simulation that provides a varying degree of pilot assistance depending on transport delays and incomplete sensory cues. This applies to both aircraft and rotorcrafts (paragraph [0002] of Dimock).

Dimock provides a Flight Simulation Training Device (FSTD) 50 including a fully functioning simulated cockpit 52 (paragraph [0027] of Dimock). Cockpit 52 itself is supported by a support frame 60 on which various actuators are disposed (paragraph [0028] of Dimock). These actuators can move simulated cockpit 52 upon instructions of a trainee inside the simulated cockpit or from a computed flight simulation system.

The flight simulation system of Dimock provides a pilot-aircraft control loop 10 having a coupling between an "objective" aircraft dynamics path 12 and a "subjective" pilot-in- the loop perception and action path 14.

According to Dimock, manually controlling an aircraft simulation involves two chains of events, connected to each other as the pilot-aircraft loop 10. First, various flight control inputs, denoted by a block 16, are received by the aircraft. Such control inputs 16 affect aircraft dynamics, denoted by a block 18. These include mechanical linkages, and possibly automation features (fly-by-wire), actuators and boosters. The aircraft simulation response as per Dimock, denoted by a block 20, symbolizes control surfaces that aerodynamically create the aircraft response as a function of its inertia and other factors. These elements introduce some form of delay between pilot input and aircraft response (paragraph [0003] of Dimock).

Dimock also represents pilot-aircraft loop 10 by various items in the pilot perception and action path 14, to be quantified by pilot perception of the aircraft response through a set of parallel sensory inputs, e.g., visual scenery 22 through cockpit windows, visual scanning of flight instruments 24, tactile perception 26, proprioceptive perception 28, vestibular perception 30, and an auditory perception (air rush, caution warnings) block 32. These parallel sensory perception inputs are fused as a pilot sensory fusion block 34 to represent a pilot reaction, denoted by a block 36. Such sensory perceptions tend to have different individual neurological delays, from milliseconds for auditory cues to hundreds of milliseconds for visual cues. In the will to achieve a specific task, the pilot reacts to the fusion of the different inputs to act on the flight controls, thereby "closing the loop" of the pilot-aircraft system.

Dimock fails to teach or suggest in-flight aircraft with a "passenger" pursuant to independent claim 1. Dimock simply aims simulation assistance depending on transport delays and incomplete sensory cues for the trainee pilot. Thus, Dimock fails to teach or suggest a passenger discomfort-aware control unit pursuant to independent claim 1.
Like Swanson, Lauwerys, and Seo, Dimock does not mention actuators adapted for inducing translational and/or rotational movements of the vehicle pursuant to independent claim

Moreover, Dimock fails to teach or suggest generating, based on sensor data, passenger discomfort-aware actuator control signals pursuant to independent claim 1. Thus, Dimock fails to teach or suggest such discomfort-aware signals for controlling motion actuators in a rotary wing aircraft that would be suitable for kinetosis reduction or for whole-body vibration reduction in passengers when being applied, pursuant to independent claim 1.
The Examiner rejected claim 11 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being obvious over Swanson in view of Seo. Claim 11 depends from independent claim 9 and is therefore patentable over Swanson in view of Seo.

The Examiner rejected claim 12 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being obvious over Swanson in view of Seo and Dimock. Claim 12 depends from independent claim 9 and is therefore patentable over Swanson in view of Seo and Dimock.

The Examiner rejected claims 13-15 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being obvious over Swanson in view of Seo and Lauwerys. Claims 13-15 depend from independent claim 9 and are therefore patentable over Swanson in view of Seo and Lauwerys.

It is believed that all stated grounds of rejection have been properly traversed, accommodated, or rendered moot. The Applicant therefore requests that the Patent Office reconsider and withdraw all presently outstanding rejections. It is believed that a full and complete response has been made to the outstanding Office Action and that the application is in condition for allowance. Thus, prompt, and favorable consideration of this amendment is requested. By addressing positions taken by the Patent Office in the above remarks, the Applicant does not acquiesce to other positions that have not been explicitly addressed. In addition, the Applicant's arguments for the patentability of a claim should not be understood as implying that no other reasons exist for the patentability of that claim.

The Applicant submits that the claims are in a condition for allowance and request a notice to that effect. If the Patent Office believes that a discussion or a claim amendment of a minor nature would advance the prosecution of this application, the Patent Office is highly encouraged to telephone the Applicant's attorney at the number given below.
